title: Get safe drinking water
short: Store it, make it safer, keep it clean
intro: Readings for when the tap water stops or may not be safe: how much to keep, how to make water safer to drink, and how to keep it clean. The pages come from the WHO and from Swiss, German, Austrian and Italian civil protection.

choices.label: Tap water is off or might be unsafe
choices.hint: A flood, a broken pipe, a warning not to drink it

read.label: Why every home needs a water reserve
read.note: In Polish. From the RCB guide: in a crisis or a war water may be hard to get; 14 litres for each person in the home is enough for a week without running water.

read.label: Boil it, or drink sealed bottled water
read.note: WHO advice after floods: boil water before you drink it or use it to brush teeth, clean wounds or prepare food; if tap water is not safe, use bottled water with its seal intact.

read.label: After a flood: before you drink from the tap
read.note: In Italian. Among the steps after a flood: check that no local notice forbids drinking tap water, and do not eat food the water touched.

choices.label: I can boil water
choices.hint: A gas stove, a camping stove, a fire

read.label: Bring it to a rolling boil, then let it cool
read.note: WHO advice: once the water is at a rolling boil, take it off the heat and let it cool without adding ice; keep hot water away from children and store it covered.

read.label: A simple filter, then boil the water
read.note: In German. An improvised sand filter for cloudy water, after which the water is boiled for about a minute.

choices.label: I have water tablets or chlorine
choices.hint: Tablets or drops from a pharmacy or a camping shop

read.label: Chlorine, bleach or tablets: the dose and the wait
read.note: A WHO table, written for travellers: prepare the product as its instructions say and add it to clear or settled water; wait at least 30 minutes at 25 °C, twice as long for every 10 °C colder.

read.label: What chlorine does not kill
read.note: From WHO's guidelines, written for water suppliers: Cryptosporidium is highly resistant to chlorine; UV light inactivates it, and filtering can remove it.

read.label: Tablets, the bathtub, and the sun
read.note: In German. Disinfecting tablets from the pharmacy, filling the bathtub as a reserve, and sun disinfection in bottles.

choices.label: No fuel and no tablets
choices.hint: Only clear bottles, sunlight, cloth or sand

read.label: Filters, and clearing cloudy water first
read.note: A WHO table, written for travellers: portable filters with pores of 1 µm or less hold back bacteria and protozoa, but the water must be clear; chlorine works best in clear or settled water.

read.label: Sun disinfection in clear bottles (SODIS)
read.note: From WHO's guidelines, written for water professionals: the SODIS method leaves water in clear plastic bottles in the sun, whose UV light, heat and oxygen together kill germs.

read.label: Sun disinfection, as an Austrian guide explains it
read.note: In German. Bottle size, how long to leave it in the sun, and how many germs it kills.

choices.label: How much water do we need?
choices.hint: Per person, per day, for how many days

read.label: At least 3 litres a person a day
read.note: In Polish. From the government's safety guide: water and ready-to-eat food at home for at least 3 days, next to a first aid kit and hygiene supplies.

read.label: The least people need in an emergency
read.note: From a WHO review: in emergencies, at least 15 litres a person a day for drinking, cooking and basic hygiene; 7.5 litres only for a short time, an absolute minimum that is not enough for hygiene.

read.label: 14 litres a person for a week
read.note: In Polish. From the RCB guide: enough for each person in the home to get through a week without running water, next to advice on storing food.

choices.label: Store water and keep it clean
choices.hint: Bottles, jerrycans, buckets, how long it keeps

read.label: Bottled water, and keeping tap water for months
read.note: In German. Why water comes first, which bottled water keeps best, and storing tap water in very clean containers, dark and cool.

read.label: Keep treated water clean
read.note: WHO advice: let boiled water cool and keep it in a clean, covered container so that it is not contaminated again.

choices.label: The power is out: will the water keep running?
choices.hint: A long power cut, the waterworks, the sewers

read.label: Without power you may lose your water
read.note: In Polish. From the government's safety guide: a power cut may last several days, and with it water, heating, the internet, phones and card payments may all stop.

read.label: First steps in a blackout: fill containers
read.note: In German. Check the stock, fill pots, buckets and bottles while water still runs, and use it sparingly.

limits.text: Treating water at home removes dirt and germs, but not chemicals.
Water that has been left to settle still needs a proven treatment before you drink it.
Chlorine does not kill every germ: Cryptosporidium, for one, is highly resistant to it.
During a flood, do not drink tap water: it may be contaminated.
After a flood, drink tap water only once no local order or notice forbids it.
Diseases carried by dirty water, such as cholera or typhoid, can kill if they are not treated.
9 litres a person cover drinking and cooking for three days, not washing or flushing the toilet.

prepare.label: How much water to keep: at least 3 litres a person a day
14 litres for each person in the home
Supplies for at least 3 days, checked every few months
Know where to turn off the water, and ask your town
prepare.note: In German. Also water for washing and flushing, not only for drinking.

prepare.label: Clean, covered containers for drinking water

learn.label: Guidelines for drinking-water quality
learn.note: WHO (2026), written for water suppliers and health authorities; its table 6.1 sets out boiling, filters and chlorine for anyone away from a safe supply.

learn.label: Domestic water quantity, service level and health
learn.note: A WHO review (2020) of how much water people need, emergencies included.

learn.label: Supplies guide
learn.note: In German. Austrian civil protection: water, food, storage, medicines.
